title: Indian Polity & Constitution
summary: The Constitution — its making, Preamble, Parts and Schedules, Rights, the three organs of government, amendments and constitutional bodies. CGL consistently asks 3-4 factual one-liners here, the single most predictable GA block.

subtopics.title: Making of the Constitution & borrowed features
subtopics.concept:
The Constituent Assembly was formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**; its members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies. It first met on **9 December 1946** in the Central Hall of Parliament with **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** as temporary chairman. **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President (11 Dec 1946); **H.C. Mukherjee** was Vice-President; **Sir B.N. Rau** was the Constitutional Adviser. Nehru's **Objective Resolution (13 Dec 1946)** became the basis of the Preamble.

### Key facts (asked again and again)
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| Time taken | 2 years, 11 months, 18 days (11 sessions) |
| Adopted | **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas) |
| Came into force | **26 January 1950** (marks Purna Swaraj Day, Lahore Session 1929) |
| Members | 389 originally, 299 after Partition; **284 signed** (24 Jan 1950) |
| Drafting Committee (29 Aug 1947) | **7 members**, chairman **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** |
| Handwritten by | Prem Behari Narain Raizada; seal showed an **Elephant** |
| Cost | About ₹64 lakh (then) |

### Important committees of the Assembly
| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Union Powers, Union Constitution, States Committees | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| Provincial Constitution Committee; Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities | Sardar Patel |
| Rules of Procedure, Steering Committee, Flag Committee | Rajendra Prasad |
| Drafting Committee | B.R. Ambedkar |

### Borrowed features (very common PYQ)
| Source country | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| **UK** | Parliamentary government, Rule of Law, single citizenship, Cabinet system, writs, bicameralism |
| **USA** | Fundamental Rights, judicial review, impeachment of President, independent judiciary, Preamble ideal |
| **Ireland** | Directive Principles (DPSP), method of electing the President, nomination of 12 members to Rajya Sabha |
| **Canada** | Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of SC |
| **Australia** | Concurrent List, freedom of inter-state trade and commerce, joint sitting of the two Houses |
| **USSR (Russia)** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble |
| **France** | Republic, ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity |
| **Germany (Weimar)** | Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency |
| **South Africa** | Procedure for amendment, election of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Japan** | Concept of "procedure established by law" |

tricks.title: Committee-chairman pairing
tricks.body: **Nehru** took the *Union/States/Constitution* committees (the 'national' subjects), **Patel** took *Provinces and Rights* (the 'practical' subjects), **Prasad** took *procedure and flag*, **Ambedkar** took the *Drafting* pen.

example.q: Who chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities?
example.solution: Sardar Patel — 'Rights' belong to Patel's practical cluster.

tricks.title: Borrowed features speed-pair
tricks.body: UK-Parliament • USA-Rights • Ireland-Duties-of-state (DPSP) • Canada-Centre-strong • Australia-List-3 • USSR-Duties-of-citizens • France-Republic • Germany-Emergency-rights • Japan-law-procedure.

example.q: Fundamental Duties are inspired by which constitution?
example.solution: USSR (Russia); the DPSP counterpart from Ireland.

mistakes: Confusing adoption date (26 Nov 1949) with enforcement date (26 Jan 1950).
Assuming Ambedkar presided over the Assembly — Rajendra Prasad did; Ambedkar chaired only the Drafting Committee.
Attributing joint sitting to Canada instead of Australia.

subtopics.title: Preamble, Parts and the 12 Schedules
subtopics.concept:
### Preamble
Text-keywords: **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic**; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity), Fraternity (dignity, unity, integrity). The words **Socialist, Secular and Integrity** were added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**. Justice ideals trace to the Russian Revolution; liberty-equality-fraternity to the French Revolution.

| Case | Holding |
|---|---|
| Berubari Union (1960) | Preamble is not a part of the Constitution |
| Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Preamble **is** a part; can be amended without altering the basic structure |
| LIC of India (1995) | Reaffirmed Preamble as an integral part |

### Parts of the Constitution (selected)
| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| I | Union and its territory | 1–4 |
| II | Citizenship | 5–11 |
| III | Fundamental Rights | 12–35 |
| IV | DPSP | 36–51 |
| IV-A | Fundamental Duties | 51A (added by 42nd, 1976) |
| V | The Union (President, Parliament, Judiciary) | 52–151 |
| VI | The States | 152–237 |
| VIII | Union Territories | 239–242 |
| IX | Panchayats | 243–243O (73rd Amendment) |
| IX-A | Municipalities | 243P–243ZG (74th Amendment) |
| IX-B | Co-operative Societies | 97th Amendment, 2011 |
| XI | Centre–State relations | 245–263 |
| XV | Elections | 324–329 |
| XVII | Official Language | 343–351 |
| XVIII | Emergency | 352–360 |
| XX | Amendment of the Constitution | 368 |

Originally **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**; today about 470 Articles and **12 Schedules**.

### The 12 Schedules
| Sch. | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Names of States and Union Territories |
| 2 | Salaries and emoluments of constitutional office holders |
| 3 | Forms of oaths and affirmations |
| 4 | Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States/UTs |
| 5 | Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes |
| 6 | Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram |
| 7 | Three Lists — Union, State, Concurrent |
| 8 | **22 recognised languages** |
| 9 | Land reform laws (added by 1st Amendment, 1951); judicial review barred till IR Coelho case (2007) |
| 10 | Anti-defection provisions (52nd Amendment, 1985) |
| 11 | **29 subjects** of Panchayats (73rd Amendment) |
| 12 | **18 subjects** of Municipalities (74th Amendment) |

Language additions to the 8th Schedule: **Sindhi** (21st Amendment, 1967); **Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali** (71st, 1992); **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali** (92nd, 2003) — total 22.

tricks.title: Preamble keyword count
tricks.body: Sovereign-Socialist-Secular-Democratic-Republic = 5 descriptors; J-L-E-F = Justice-Liberty-Equality-Fraternity, with only Justice split three ways (social-economic-political).

example.q: Which Preamble ideal is described in three parts?
example.solution: Justice — social, economic and political (Russian Revolution inspiration).

mistakes: Saying the Preamble was amended by the 44th — it was the 42nd (1976).
Listing 18 languages — the count has been 22 since the 92nd Amendment (2003).
Mixing up the 9th Schedule (land reform laws) with the 10th (defection).

subtopics.title: Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Fundamental Duties
subtopics.concept:
### Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12–35)
Justiciable rights against the State (Art. 12). Six categories after the Right to Property was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment (1978)** and made a legal right under **Article 300A**.

| Right | Articles | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Equality | 14–18 | 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination; 16 equal opportunity in public jobs; 17 abolition of untouchability; 18 abolition of titles |
| Freedom | 19–22 | Art. 19 now has **six** freedoms (property removed); 20 protection on conviction; **21 life and personal liberty** (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978); **21A education for ages 6–14** (86th Amendment, 2002); 22 arrest and detention safeguards |
| Against exploitation | 23–24 | Ban on human trafficking and forced labour; no child below 14 in factories |
| Religion | 25–28 | Freedom of conscience and religion; secular state |
| Cultural and educational | 29–30 | Minority rights to conserve language, script, culture |
| Constitutional remedies | **32** | Writs; called the **"heart and soul" of the Constitution by Ambedkar** |

EWS reservation of **10%** added via **103rd Amendment (2019)** — Articles 15(6) and 16(6).

### Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36–51)
Non-justiciable; borrowed from **Ireland**. Classified: Socialist (38, 39, 41, 42, 43), Gandhian (40 village panchayats, 43, 46, 47 prohibition, 48 cow protection), Liberal-intellectual (44 **Uniform Civil Code**, 45, 50, 51 international peace). Added later: 39A free legal aid, 43A worker participation, 48A environment (all by 42nd Amendment); Art. 45 rewritten by 86th Amendment (early childhood care).

### Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A)
Recommended by the **Swaran Singh Committee (1976)**; **10 duties added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)**; the **11th duty** (parents/guardians to provide education opportunities to children aged 6–14) added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**. Inspired by the **USSR** constitution. Non-justiciable; apply only to citizens.

tricks.title: FR article blocks
tricks.body: 14-18 Equality • 19-22 Freedom • 23-24 Exploitation • 25-28 Religion • 29-30 Culture-Education • 32 Remedies. Count blocks as 5+4+2+4+2+1.

example.q: Under which article is the abolition of untouchability placed?
example.solution: Article 17 — the first article of the Equality block (14-18).

tricks.title: Duty amendment pair
tricks.body: 42nd gave 10 duties; 86th added the 11th (education of 6-14 year-olds). Same 86th also inserted Art. 21A — one amendment, twin gifts.

example.q: Which amendment added the 11th Fundamental Duty?

mistakes: Treating the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right — it is now Art. 300A, a legal right.
Thinking all FRs suspend in a national emergency — Arts. 20 and 21 never suspend.
Believing DPSPs are enforceable in court — they are non-justiciable.

subtopics.title: Union and State Executive
subtopics.concept:
### The President (Articles 52–62)
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Election | Indirect: elected MPs + elected MLAs of States, Delhi and Puducherry; single transferable vote, proportional representation; secret ballot |
| Qualification | Citizen, 35 years, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member |
| Oath | Administered by the **Chief Justice of India** (Art. 60) |
| Term / impeachment | 5 years; removal for "violation of the Constitution" (Art. 61) — charge by either House with 2/3 of total membership, other House investigates; 14 days' notice |
| Pardon power (Art. 72) | Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation; also in **court-martial** cases and death sentences |
| Current (as on 23 Sep 2026) | **Droupadi Murmu, 15th President** (since 25 July 2022; first tribal President) |

### The Vice-President (Articles 63–71)
Elected by **all members (elected + nominated) of both Houses** — the only office whose electoral college includes nominated MPs. Ex-officio **Chairman of Rajya Sabha**. Removal: resolution initiated only in **Rajya Sabha (effective majority)** and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)). **C.P. Radhakrishnan is the 15th Vice-President (since 12 September 2025)**.

### Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (Articles 74–75)
- Art. 74: CoM **to aid and advise** the President; Art. 75: appointment, collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**.
- **91st Amendment (2003)**: CoM capped at **15%** of Lok Sabha / State Assembly strength; defectors barred from ministership.

### The Governor (Articles 153–162)
Appointed by the President for 5 years (holds office at pleasure); pardon power under **Art. 161** (no court-martial power, cannot pardon death sentence); can **reserve bills for the President (Art. 200–201)**; ordinance power **Art. 213**.

tricks.title: Electoral college contrast
tricks.body: President = elected MPs + elected MLAs (no nominated). Vice-President = ALL MPs of both Houses, including the 12 nominated. 'Vice' reaches where 'President' does not.

example.q: Do nominated members of the Rajya Sabha vote in the Vice-Presidential election?
example.solution: Yes — they are excluded only from the President's electoral college.

tricks.title: Pardon ladder
tricks.body: President's Art. 72 pardons court-martial and death sentences; the Governor's Art. 161 covers neither. 'Governor = softer ladder'.

example.q: Can a Governor pardon a death sentence?

mistakes: Saying the President takes oath from the Vice-President — the CJI administers it.
Assuming the VP's removal starts in the Lok Sabha — it starts in the Rajya Sabha (Art. 67(b)).
Forgetting the 91st Amendment's 15% minister cap and attributing it to anti-defection's 52nd.

subtopics.title: Parliament and the Judiciary
subtopics.concept:
### Parliament (Articles 79–122)
- **Lok Sabha**: max **530** state seats (the 2 nominated Anglo-Indian seats ended with the 104th Amendment, 2020); term 5 years. Speaker: elected from among members; casting vote; certifies a **Money Bill** (Art. 110); presides over **joint sittings**; pro-tem Speaker appointed by the President to administer oaths. Current Speaker: **Om Birla** (18th Lok Sabha).
- **Rajya Sabha**: max 250 (238 elected + **12 nominated by the President** — literature, science, art, social service); permanent house, one-third retire every 2 years; Deputy Chairman presides in the House.
- **Sessions**: Budget (Feb–May), Monsoon (Jul–Sep), Winter (Nov–Dec). Gap between sessions cannot exceed **6 months**. Quorum: **1/10th** of membership.
- **Joint sitting (Art. 108)**: not for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills; held only **three times** — Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), POTA (2002).
- Bills: Ordinary, Money, Financial, Constitutional Amendment (Art. 368). **Ordinance power — Art. 123** (ordinance lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles).

### Key committees
| Committee | Strength | Chairman |
|---|---|---|
| Public Accounts Committee | 22 (15 LS + 7 RS) | By convention from the **Opposition**; examines CAG reports |
| Estimates Committee | 30 (all Lok Sabha) | From the ruling party |
| Committee on Public Undertakings | 22 (15 LS + 7 RS) | — |

### Judiciary
- **Supreme Court (Art. 124)**: sanctioned strength **34 judges**; retirement **65** (HC: 62); judges removed by Parliament on "proved misbehaviour or incapacity" via the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 (special majority). Appointments through the **collegium** (Second Judges case 1993). Current CJI: **Justice Surya Kant (53rd CJI, since 24 November 2025)**.
- Jurisdictions: original (Art. 131), writs (32), appellate (132–136), **SLP Art. 136**, review (137), advisory (143), **law of the land binding (Art. 141)**, complete justice (142). Court of record: Art. 129.
- **High Courts: 25**; writ power of HCs (**Art. 226**) is wider than the SC's — it covers fundamental **and other legal rights**. Oldest HCs: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1862).

### Writs
| Writ | Meaning | Against |
|---|---|---|
| Habeas corpus | "Produce the body" — release from illegal detention | State/individual |
| Mandamus | "We command" — perform public duty | Public official |
| Prohibition | Stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction | Judicial/quasi-judicial |
| Certiorari | Transfers/quashes an order of a lower court | Judicial/quasi-judicial |
| Quo warranto | "By what authority" — challenges illegal occupation of a public office | Public office holder |

tricks.title: Committee trio numbers
tricks.body: PAC 22 (opposition chair), CPU 22 (15+7), Estimates 30 (all LS). 'Estimates = 30, exclusively LS.'

example.q: Which parliamentary committee examines the CAG's reports?
example.solution: The Public Accounts Committee (22 members, opposition chairperson by convention).

tricks.title: Writ first letters
tricks.body: **H-M-P-C-Q**: Habeas(body), Mandamus(command), Prohibition(stop-before), Certiorari(quash-after), Quo warranto(by what authority). Prohibition stops a case early; certiorari quashes after.

example.q: Which writ stops a subordinate court from exceeding jurisdiction before it decides?
example.solution: Prohibition (certiorari operates after the order is passed).

mistakes: Believing a joint sitting can resolve a Constitutional Amendment Bill — Art. 108 excludes it.
Saying the Rajya Sabha can be dissolved — it is permanent, with one-third retiring every two years.
Assuming the sanctioned SC strength is 31 — it rose to 34 in 2019.

subtopics.title: Important Constitutional Amendments
subtopics.concept:
Procedure: **Article 368** — simple majority for some (outside Art. 368), **special majority** for most; ratification by **half the State legislatures** for federal provisions (election of President, extent of executive power, SC/HC, representation of states, 7th Schedule, Art. 368 itself). The **basic structure doctrine** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits amendment power.

### Important amendments (PYQ bank)
| Am. | Year | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951 | Added 9th Schedule; reasonable restrictions on FRs; Arts. 31A, 31B |
| 7th | 1956 | States reorganisation; abolished A/B/C/D class states |
| 24th | 1971 | Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights |
| 42nd | 1976 | "Mini-Constitution": Socialist-Secular-Integrity in Preamble; Fundamental Duties; education, forests, wildlife to Concurrent List; LS term 5→6 yrs (reverted by 44th) |
| 44th | 1978 | Deleted Right to Property (Art. 300A); "armed rebellion" replaced "internal disturbance" in Art. 352 |
| 52nd | 1985 | Anti-defection law — Tenth Schedule |
| 61st | 1988 | Voting age **21 → 18** |
| 65th | 1990 | National Commission for SC/ST (Art. 338) |
| 69th | 1991 | Delhi named National Capital Territory; own Assembly |
| 71st | 1992 | Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali added to 8th Schedule |
| 73rd / 74th | 1992 | Constitutional status to Panchayats / Municipalities; 11th & 12th Schedules |
| 86th | 2002 | Art. 21A — Right to Education; 11th Fundamental Duty |
| 89th | 2003 | Separate National Commission for ST (Art. 338A) |
| 91st | 2003 | CoM limited to 15% of House strength |
| 92nd | 2003 | Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali added — 22 languages |
| 97th | 2011 | Co-operative societies; Part IX-B |
| 99th | 2014 | NJAC (struck down in 2015) |
| 100th | 2015 | India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement |
| 101st | 2016 | **GST**; Art. 279A GST Council |
| 102nd | 2018 | Constitutional status to National Commission for Backward Classes (Art. 338B) |
| 103rd | 2019 | **10% EWS reservation** (Arts. 15(6), 16(6)) |
| 104th | 2020 | Extended SC/ST reservation in legislatures 10 years; ended Anglo-Indian nominated seats |
| 105th | 2021 | Restored States' power to identify OBCs (Art. 342A) |
| 106th | 2023 | **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam** — 1/3rd seats for women in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (to take effect after delimitation following a census) |

tricks.title: Amendment decade clusters
tricks.body: 1950s structural (1st, 7th) • 1970s power (24, 42, 44) • 1980s politics (52 anti-defection, 61 voting age) • 1990s grass-roots (73, 74) + language (71, 92) • 2000s rights (86, 91, 97) • 2010s-20s economy-equality (101 GST, 102 OBC, 103 EWS, 104 seats, 105 OBC-identify, 106 women).

example.q: Which amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18?

tricks.title: 42 vs 44 tug-of-war
tricks.body: Whatever the 42nd tightened, the 44th loosened: term 6→5 years, 'internal disturbance'→'armed rebellion', property FR→300A legal right.

example.q: Which amendment changed the ground for National Emergency from 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion'?

mistakes: Attributing EWS (10%) to the 102nd — it is the 103rd; the 102nd made NCBC constitutional.
Assuming the 106th applies at once — it awaits delimitation after a census.
Thinking NJAC still operates — the 99th Amendment was struck down in 2015.

subtopics.title: Panchayati Raj, Municipalities and Emergency
subtopics.concept:
### Panchayati Raj committees (very common PYQ)
| Committee | Year | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Balwant Rai Mehta** | 1957 | **Three-tier** PR system; led to launch at **Nagaur, Rajasthan on 2 Oct 1959** (then Andhra Pradesh) |
| **Ashok Mehta** | 1977 | **Two-tier** system — Zila Parishad + Mandal Panchayat; district as first point of decentralisation |
| **G.V.K. Rao** | 1985 | District the basic unit of planning — District Development Commissioner |
| **L.M. Singhvi** | 1986 | **Constitutional status** for PRIs; Nyaya Panchayats |

### 73rd Amendment (1992) — Panchayats (Part IX, Arts. 243–243O, 11th Schedule)
Three-tier system (two-tier if State population below 20 lakh); **Gram Sabha (243A)**; reservation for SC/ST in proportion and **not less than 1/3rd for women** (many States have raised it to 50% — Bihar first, 2006); 5-year term; **State Election Commission (243K)**; **State Finance Commission every 5 years (243I)**; **29 subjects** in the 11th Schedule.

### 74th Amendment (1992) — Municipalities (Part IX-A, 12th Schedule)
Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation; **18 subjects**; same reservation pattern; District/Metropolitan Planning Committees (243ZD/243ZE).

### Emergency provisions (Part XVIII)
| Type | Article | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| National | **352** | Proclaimed **3 times** — 1962 (China), 1971 (Pakistan), 1975 ("internal disturbance", now "armed rebellion" per 44th Amdt). Approval within **1 month**, renewal every **6 months**; LS can revoke by simple majority; FRs of Art. 19 auto-suspend (Art. 358); only Arts. 20–21 never suspend (Art. 359) |
| President's Rule | **356** | First used in **1959 (Kerala)**; imposed over 130 times; 6-month approval, max **3 years** (conditions after 1 year per **S.R. Bommai case, 1994** — floor test, judicial review) |
| Financial | **360** | **Never imposed** so far |

tricks.title: Committee tier-count rhyme
tricks.body: Balwant-3 (1957), Ashok-2 (1977), Rao-district (1985), Singhvi-Constitution (1986). Decade rhyme: 57-77-85-86.

example.q: Which committee's report led to the Nagaur (Rajasthan) launch of Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959?
example.solution: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (three-tier recommendation).

tricks.title: Emergency digits
tricks.body: 352-National (3 proclamations: 62, 71, 75), 356-President's Rule (Kerala 1959 first), 360-Financial (zero uses). Approvals: 1 month + every 6 months.

example.q: Which State first faced President's Rule in 1959?
example.solution: Kerala (the elected E.M.S. Namboodiripad government was dismissed).

mistakes: Saying the 73rd Amendment created the Panchayats in 1959 — the 1959 date is only Rajasthan's launch; constitutional status came in 1992.
Mixing 11th Schedule (29 subjects, panchayats) with 12th (18, municipalities).
Claiming a Financial Emergency was declared in 1991 — Art. 360 has never been used.

subtopics.title: Constitutional & Statutory Bodies (with current heads)
subtopics.concept:
### Constitutional vs statutory bodies — with current heads (as on 23 September 2026)
| Body | Article / Act | Nature | Current head (2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Election Commission | **Art. 324** | Constitutional | **CEC Gyanesh Kumar** (26th CEC, since Feb 2025); CEC + 2 ECs; CEC removable like a SC judge; appointments now under the CEC and Other ECs (Appointment etc.) Act, 2023 — PM + LoP (LS) + a Union Minister |
| UPSC | **Arts. 315–323** | Constitutional | **Dr. Ajay Kumar** (Chairman since 15 May 2025); members hold office for 6 years or till 65 |
| CAG | **Art. 148** | Constitutional | **K. Sanjay Murthy** (15th CAG, since Nov 2024); term 6 years or 65; audits accounts; reports go to the President/Governor and are examined by the **PAC** |
| Attorney General | **Art. 76** | Constitutional office | **R. Venkataramani** (16th AG; extended till 30 Sep 2027); right to speak in Parliament, no vote |
| Finance Commission | **Art. 280** | Constitutional | **16th FC — Dr. Arvind Panagariya**; report tabled **1 Feb 2026**; award period **2026–31**; recommends States' share — **41%** of the divisible pool (same as 15th FC) |
| NITI Aayog | 1 Jan 2015 (Cabinet resolution) | **Neither constitutional nor statutory** | Chair: PM; Vice-Chair: **A.K. Lahiri** (May 2026); CEO: **Anurag Jain** (Aug 2026); replaced the Planning Commission (1950) |
| NHRC | Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (amended 2019) | Statutory | **Justice V. Ramasubramanian** (since Dec 2024); chair is a former CJI or SC judge |
| Central Information Commission | RTI Act, 2005 | Statutory | **Raj Kumar Goyal** (CIC since 15 Dec 2025); CIC + up to 10 Information Commissioners |
| Central Vigilance Commission | CVCA, 2003 | Statutory | Supervises CBI's work under the Prevention of Corruption Act |
| Lokpal | Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 | Statutory | **Justice A.M. Khanwilkar** (Chair since Mar 2024); first chair: Justice P.C. Ghose (2019) |

Key contrasts often asked: **CAG** — ineligible for further Government office after term; **UPSC chairman** — also ineligible; **SPSC chairman** can be made a UPSC member; **AG** is not a full-time government servant; **NITI Aayog** has no statutory backing while the Finance Commission is mandated every **five years**.

example.q: Under which article is the Comptroller and Auditor General appointed?

tricks.title: Statutory vs constitutional filter
tricks.body: If the source is a dated Act (1993 NHRC, 2003 CVC, 2005 CIC, 2013 Lokpal) it is statutory; if the source is an Article number it is constitutional; NITI Aayog (Cabinet resolution, 2015) is neither.

example.q: Name one high-profile advisory body that is neither constitutional nor statutory.

mistakes: Calling NITI Aayog a statutory body — it is an executive-resolution body.
Saying the 15th FC still governs transfers — from FY 2026-27 the 16th FC (41% share, 2026-31) applies.
Confusing the CAG's examiners — CAG reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee, not the Estimates Committee.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four pairs given, one correct — e.g. Schedule with subject, amendment with provision.
pyqPatterns.approach: Eliminate pairs you know are wrong; the surviving option is the answer. Focus on 42nd/44th/73rd/101st/103rd/106th.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Current head of a constitutional body
pyqPatterns.approach: Memorise the current-heads table; update after every appointment news cycle.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'X feature is taken from which country?'
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the 10-country speed-pair list; watch for Canada-vs-Australia and Ireland-vs-USSR traps.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Which is NOT a Fundamental Right / DPSP classification
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One odd option inside a list of rights (usually property, or a duty disguised as a right).
pyqPatterns.approach: Remember property left Part III in 1978; check the article block numbers.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Direct ask: 'The ... Amendment lowered voting age / added GST / reserved seats for women.'
pyqPatterns.approach: Learn the amendment table as year+keyword flashcards.
Tier-count mnemonic (Balwant-3, Ashok-2) plus Assembly-committee chairman clusters.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Consider the following statements...' with options like '1 and 2 only'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test each statement against a known article; usually one statement is an absolute (always/only) trap.
Anchor each power to its article; note President-vs-Governor differences.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following features of the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from Australia?
options: Federal system with a strong Centre
solvedExamples.solution: The **Concurrent List** (and freedom of inter-state trade, joint sitting) came from **Australia**. Fundamental Rights and judicial review came from the USA, DPSP from Ireland, and a strong-Centre federation from Canada.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mnemonic for Australia — **CAJ**: Concurrent list, Joint sitting, trade And commerce.

solvedExamples.q:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly:
1. It held its first meeting on 9 December 1946.
2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was its permanent President.
3. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949.

Which of the statements are correct?
solvedExamples.solution: The Assembly first met on 9 Dec 1946 and adopted the Constitution on 26 Nov 1949 — both correct. Its permanent President was **Dr. Rajendra Prasad**; Ambedkar only chaired the **Drafting Committee**. So statements 1 and 3 are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Ambedkar = Drafting (D), Prasad = President (P) — both start with the right letters.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following statements about the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 is correct?
options: It restored the term of the Lok Sabha to five years
It deleted the Right to Property from Part III
It added the words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble
It placed education in the State List
solvedExamples.solution: The 42nd Amendment (called the **Mini-Constitution**) added **Socialist, Secular and Integrity** to the Preamble, inserted Fundamental Duties, moved education/forests/wildlife to the **Concurrent** List and made the Lok Sabha term six years. The term was restored to five years and property was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following bodies is neither a constitutional nor a statutory body?
solvedExamples.solution: **NITI Aayog** (1 January 2015) was created by a **Cabinet resolution** — it has no constitutional article or Act behind it. ECI (Art. 324), Finance Commission (Art. 280) and UPSC (Art. 315) are constitutional bodies; NHRC, CVC, CIC and Lokpal are statutory.
solvedExamples.shortcut: NITI = 'no instrument of law' — think executive-only body.

practice.q: The method of election of the President of India and the Directive Principles of State Policy have been borrowed from which country?
practice.solution: Both the DPSP and the method of electing the President (indirect election through an electoral college) were taken from the **Constitution of Ireland**. Ireland also gave the provision for nominating 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
practice.shortcut: Ireland = 'President + Principles' — both P-words pair up.

practice.q: The words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added to the Preamble by which Amendment?
practice.solution: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** added these three words to the Preamble and is called the 'Mini-Constitution'. The 44th Amendment later undid several 42nd changes (e.g. property, emergency grounds).
practice.shortcut: SS + I = Socialist, Secular, Integrity — all from '42', the SS regiment number rhyme (SS ~ 42 in shape).

practice.q: Which Article was described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Indian Constitution?
options: Article 21 — Protection of life and personal liberty
practice.solution: Ambedkar called **Article 32** (writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court) the heart and soul of the Constitution because it makes the Fundamental Rights actually enforceable. Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto flow from it.

practice.q: How many languages are presently recognised in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution?
practice.solution: **22 languages** — Sindhi (21st Amdt, 1967), Konkani-Manipuri-Nepali (71st Amdt, 1992) and Bodo-Dogri-Maithili-Santhali (92nd Amdt, 2003) took the count from 14 to 22.

practice.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and that too on the recommendation of the President.
2. The Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is final.
3. A Constitutional Amendment Bill can be passed at a joint sitting of both Houses.

Which of the statements are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct (Arts. 109, 110). Joint sittings (Art. 108) are **not** available for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills, so statement 3 is wrong. Only three joint sittings have ever been held (1961, 1978, 2002).
practice.shortcut: Remember the two 'excluded' bills: Money and Constitution-amendment — Art. 108 skips both.

practice.q: The writ of 'quo warranto' is issued to:
options: release a person from illegal detention
direct a public official to perform his duty
question the legality of a person holding a public office
quash the order of a lower court
practice.solution: **Quo warranto** literally means 'by what authority' — it prevents a person from unlawfully occupying a public office. Release from illegal detention is *habeas corpus*; commanding performance of duty is *mandamus*; quashing a lower court's order is *certiorari*.
practice.shortcut: warranto ~ 'where is your warrant to hold this post?'

practice.q: As of September 2026, who is the Chief Justice of India?
practice.solution: **Justice Surya Kant** is the **53rd CJI**, sworn in on **24 November 2025** (tenure runs to February 2027). B.R. Gavai (52nd) and Sanjiv Khanna (51st) were his immediate predecessors; D.Y. Chandrachud retired in November 2024.

practice.q: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 provides for:
options: one-third reservation for women in the Rajya Sabha
one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies
50% reservation for women in Panchayati Raj institutions
practice.solution: The **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023)** reserves **one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies** for women; it takes effect after a delimitation following the next census. EWS (10%) was the 103rd Amendment; 1/3rd in PRIs came with the 73rd Amendment.

practice.q: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Finance Commission — a statutory body under Article 280
16th Finance Commission — Arvind Panagariya; award period 2026–31
14th Finance Commission — raised States' share to 41%
practice.solution: The **16th Finance Commission** (chair: **Arvind Panagariya**) covers **2026-27 to 2030-31**; its report was tabled on 1 Feb 2026 recommending a **41%** States' share. The 15th FC covered 2021–26; the Finance Commission is a **constitutional** body; the 14th FC had raised the share to **42%**.
practice.shortcut: Odd-one-out elimination: 15th FC = 2021–26; FC is constitutional; 14th FC = 42% — only option (c) survives.

practice.q: Under Article 243-I, a State Finance Commission is constituted once in how many years?
practice.solution: A **State Finance Commission every five years** (Art. 243-I) reviews the financial position of panchayats and municipalities, on the lines of the central Finance Commission (Art. 280).
practice.shortcut: FC (centre) and SFC (state) both run on 5-year cycles.

practice.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right under the Constitution of India?
options: Right to move freely throughout the territory of India
practice.solution: The **Right to Property** was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment, 1978** and is now only a **legal right under Article 300A**. The others are Fundamental Rights (Arts. 23–24, 19(1)(d) and 32).
practice.shortcut: 'Property' left the FR list in 1978 — the year of the 44th.
practice.pattern: which is NOT a fundamental right

practice.q: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 capped the strength of the Council of Ministers at what percentage of the strength of the Lok Sabha (or a State Assembly)?
practice.solution: The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the Council of Ministers to **15%** of the total strength of the Lok Sabha / State Legislative Assembly; it also barred defectors from becoming ministers.
practice.shortcut: 91 ~ 15: think '91st minute of a match, 15 minutes left'.

practice.q: Which committee recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system consisting of Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat?
practice.solution: The **Ashok Mehta Committee (1977)** suggested a **two-tier** scheme — Zila Parishad at the district and Mandal Panchayat (cluster of villages) below it. Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) had recommended **three tiers**, G.V.K. Rao (1985) wanted the district as the planning unit, and L.M. Singhvi (1986) sought constitutional status.
practice.shortcut: Tier count mnemonic: Balwant-3, Ashok-2 ('B-A = 3-2'), Rao-district, Singhvi-Constitution.

practice.q: The Vice-President of India can be removed by a resolution:
options: passed by the Lok Sabha with a special majority
initiated in the Lok Sabha and agreed to by the Rajya Sabha
of the Rajya Sabha by an effective majority, agreed to by the Lok Sabha
passed by both Houses with a two-thirds majority of total membership
practice.solution: Under **Art. 67(b)**, removal is by a resolution of the **Rajya Sabha passed by an effective majority** (majority of that House's total strength), **agreed to by the Lok Sabha**, with 14 days' notice. The VP is not impeached; he also doubles as Rajya Sabha Chairman, hence removal starts in that House.
practice.shortcut: VP removal = RS-first (he chairs the RS), unlike the President's impeachment which can start in either House.

practice.q: Which of the following statements about a Financial Emergency under Article 360 is correct?
options: It has never been proclaimed in India so far
It was proclaimed once, during the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis
It can be proclaimed only on the recommendation of the Rajya Sabha
It automatically ceases after one year
practice.solution: A Financial Emergency (**Art. 360**) has **never been imposed** in India. The 1991 crisis was handled through economic reforms, not Art. 360. Unlike other emergencies there is no automatic one-year expiry provision of the kind stated in option (d); approval and periodic renewal follow Art. 352-style parliamentary approval.
